slides.title: Browser Session
slides.subtitle: Join a controlled browser to an existing Session with a one-use signed assertion
slides.notes: PAP can carry one Session across APIs, conversations and the company's website. This example shows how a browser the agent controls joins the Session the agent already has.

slides.title: Why a Browser Session
slides.statement: One Session, on the **API** and on the **website**: the same user, the same sign-in, the same scopes.
slides.notes: Sometimes the agent needs a company web page, say to confirm an operation. Instead of signing in again, the browser joins the Session the agent already holds.

slides.title: Who takes part

columns.heading: Personal agent
columns.content: Builds a short-lived **browser assertion**, signed by the **Reactor signer**.

columns.heading: Agent-controlled browser
columns.content: POSTs the assertion in a top-level form. **Not** the user's ordinary browser.

columns.heading: Company
columns.content: Its `web.browser_session_endpoint` verifies it, accepts its `jti` once, sets a cookie.

slides.notes: The agent signs the assertion through Reactor. A browser it controls posts it to the endpoint that discovery advertised. The company verifies the assertion, records it in a replay cache, and sets its own Session cookie.

slides.title: Joining the Session

items.title: Sign
items.detail: iss, pairwise sub, session_id, jti; typ poppy-browser+jwt

items.title: POST
items.detail: The assertion, in the form body

items.title: Verify
items.detail: Signature, audience, owner, lifetime, one use

slides.notes: The agent checks the endpoint and where it will return to, builds the claims and signs them with the distinct type poppy-browser+jwt. The browser posts it. The company verifies it, accepts the jti once, answers 303 with a cookie, and the browser lands on the requested page.

slides.title: Agent responsibilities
items: The advertised HTTPS endpoint is the exact audience
`return_to` only on the company's domain or a subdomain
The pairwise User ID and Session ID that belong together
At most **60 seconds** of life; a `jti` of at least 128 bits
A top-level form POST: never a query string, never the user's browser
slides.notes: BrowserSessionClient resolves the clock, randomness, signing and the form POST through Reactor. It returns only the endpoint, the safe return location and the expiry; the compact assertion never leaves the host.

slides.title: Company responsibilities
items: ES256 or RS256 signature against the agent's verified JWKS
Expected client, pairwise User ID, active Session, safe return target
Atomic one-use acceptance of `(client_id, jti)` until expiry
slides.notes: verify_browser_assertion in Python and verifyBrowserAssertion in TypeScript's server entry do these checks, including a lifetime of 60 seconds at most. Creating the cookie is left to the company's web framework, on purpose.

slides.title: The company's cookie
slides.statement: `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite` Lax or None, and it **never outlives** the PAP Session.
slides.notes: The cookie follows later sign-in, sign-out and scope changes. In the reference companies, the __Host-poppy_session cookie has no lifetime of its own, so signing out reaches the website on its next request.

slides.title: What stays where

left.heading: Never in a URL or model context

slides.notes: The assertion travels only in the form body, from the agent's own browser. What the model gets back is the endpoint, where the browser landed, and yes-or-no evidence that each rule held.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples sign a real ES256 assertion, verify it, then replay it and see it refused
slides.notes: Both examples pass a real assertion through a Reactor form POST contribution, verify it, and submit it a second time to show replay rejection. Upstream's Web browsing section has the rules in full.
